title: Spurious liquor toll in Manipur's Chandel rises to 16; six arrested, nearly 600 treated
dek: Police say six people have been arrested over the supply of the suspected spurious liquor, and the state has set up a high-level inquiry committee. Doctors suspect methanol poisoning.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Sixteen people have died and nearly 600 have been treated in hospital after drinking suspected spurious liquor in Manipur's Chandel district, police said on Saturday, after three more deaths during the day. Six people have been arrested for their alleged role in supplying the liquor, and the state government has set up a high-level inquiry committee, according to a police statement. It is one of the deadliest suspected liquor poisonings in the north-east in recent years.

"The cumulative toll from Chandel district is 16," Inspector General of Police Themthing Ngahsangva said, adding that "nearly 600 people" were being treated at private and government hospitals, according to reports. Police are still tracing where the liquor came from. Doctors treating patients in Imphal say the symptoms point to methanol poisoning, but officials say the cause has not yet been medically established.

The victims are mostly men, many of them cultivators, from villages in the Chakpikarong and Chandel subdivisions near the state's border with Myanmar. Police say the liquor was bought in Sugnu, a village in neighbouring Kakching district, and was not brewed in Chandel. Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh has ordered an enquiry and said those responsible "will be punished", according to reports. Teams from the district administration, police, excise and health departments visited Sugnu, Chakpikarong and the hospitals treating victims on Saturday, according to reports.

## What happened

The first deaths were reported on Tuesday and Wednesday. A medical officer at the Chakpikarong Health Centre said on Thursday that at least six people had died over two days with breathing difficulties, severe abdominal pain and restlessness, and that the deaths appeared to be poisoning, but that the link with alcohol could not be confirmed because the patients had died before they could be treated or diagnosed, according to reports. The officer said two more people had died with similar symptoms in the preceding weeks.

By Friday, an official communication from Chandel's superintendent of police had confirmed eight deaths, according to reports. Earlier on Saturday the chief minister said the toll "has touched 11 during the last 48 hours"; by the evening police put it at 16. Most of the dead were aged between 32 and 50, one report said.

The number of people needing treatment is larger, and the figures differ. The chief minister said more than 140 patients had been admitted to Shija Hospital at Lamphelpat and more than 41 to Babina Hospital at Sajiwa, both on the outskirts of Imphal. Shija Hospitals said separately that it had attended to more than 312 patients for methanol poisoning, a figure that includes people who were examined but not admitted. Others were taken to the state's two big public hospitals, the Regional Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS) and the Jawaharlal Nehru Institute of Medical Sciences (JNIMS). Some patients are on haemodialysis, and hospitals in Imphal reported a shortage of beds for patients needing it, according to reports.

Chetan K, joint managing director of Shija Hospitals, said patients had come in with dizziness, stomach pain and other complications, according to reports. A doctor at JNIMS said many people who had drunk local liquor had come to hospital out of fear, which helps explain the gap between the number treated and the number admitted.

## The investigation

In a letter to Chandel's deputy commissioner, Mamoni Doley, the district superintendent of police, Dharmendra Kumar, identified Sugnu as the place where the liquor was reportedly bought, according to reports. Five of the deaths fall under the jurisdiction of the Sugnu police station. A special investigation team is tracing how the liquor was made and moved, one report said.

Sugnu, a few kilometres from the affected villages, is known for brewing local liquor, and it came under scrutiny as soon as the first deaths were reported. The officer in charge of the Chakpikarong police station, M. Poukhilung Rongmei, said on Thursday that police were taking the situation seriously and would hold awareness camps, and urged people to be careful with locally brewed liquor, according to reports.

## The government's response

Mr Singh visited patients at Shija and Babina hospitals on Friday afternoon and said he had told hospital authorities to ensure "the best possible medical care", according to reports. A medical team led by a general medicine specialist was sent to Chandel with essential medicines, and four rapid response teams have been deployed in the district, according to reports.

The district administrations of Chandel, Imphal West and Kakching issued a joint health advisory telling people not to drink locally brewed liquor or liquor of doubtful origin, especially from the suspected source. It urged anyone who had drunk such liquor to seek medical care at once, even without symptoms, if they had vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, blurred vision or difficulty breathing. Methanol poisoning can take hours to show symptoms, and early treatment, including dialysis, can prevent blindness and death. The Chandel administration has banned the sale of unverified local liquor, one report said.

Chandel's MLA, S.S. Olish, said arrangements were being made to move more patients to Imphal and that the chief minister had been asked to look into the situation, according to reports. Party workers in Chakpikarong were arranging vehicles to take patients to hospital.

## Background

Manipur was a dry state for more than three decades under the Manipur Liquor Prohibition Act of 1991, passed after sustained campaigns by women's groups and civil society against alcoholism and domestic violence. The law still allowed Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe communities to brew liquor for traditional purposes, and illicit brewing remained widespread.

Prohibition was eased in stages. The hill districts were exempted in 2002, and in September 2022 the cabinet allowed sale in district headquarters and larger hotels. In December 2023 the cabinet approved the manufacture, sale and possession of liquor more widely, saying regulation would bring in revenue and curb spurious drinks that harm health. Civil society groups opposed the move. A state-owned company, the Manipur State Beverages Corporation, was set up to oversee production and distribution.

The deaths have renewed questions about how locally made liquor is regulated and checked in the state, according to reports. Manipur has been under strain since ethnic violence broke out in May 2023, and its police and health services have been stretched.

Methanol, a toxic industrial alcohol, is sometimes added to illicit liquor to increase its strength cheaply, or is produced by poor distillation. Similar poisonings have killed scores of people in other states in recent years.

## What happens next

The high-level inquiry committee has not been given a deadline in public, and police have not named those arrested. Laboratory tests on samples of the liquor and on patients will be needed to confirm whether methanol caused the deaths. Doctors say the number of deaths may rise because several patients are in a serious condition.

## Key numbers

- 16 deaths, according to police on Saturday evening
- Nearly 600 people treated in hospital, according to police
- 6 people arrested over the supply of the liquor
- More than 180 patients admitted to two Imphal hospitals, according to the chief minister
- More than 312 patients attended to at Shija Hospitals, according to the hospital
- 4 rapid response medical teams deployed in Chandel district
- 1991: year Manipur's liquor prohibition law was passed; 2023: cabinet approves wider lifting
